titulo: First Steps in German: Read German with Confidence

aula.objetivo: By the end of this lesson, understand a short exchange, distinguish key German sounds from English, decode common spelling patterns and greet someone confidently.

blocos.texto: Yesterday you learned that German letters do not always behave like English letters. Today you will become a word detective: look at a word, predict the sound of its letter combinations, then check your prediction against the audio. The win is decoding a new word without a phonetic crutch.

blocos.titulo: The four patterns that unlock dozens of words
blocos.explicacao: STEP 1: German «ei» sounds /aɪ/, like eye: «Wein» and «Eis». STEP 2: German «ie» usually represents long /iː/, as in English see: «Bier» and «Brief». STEP 3: German «eu» and «äu» are pronounced /ɔʏ/, roughly like oy in boy: «Euro» and «Häuser». STEP 4: German «au» sounds /aʊ/, like ow in cow: «Haus» and «Auto». Now compare «Wein» and «Wien»: the spelling difference changes both sound and meaning. The patterns are reliable guides for these common words, not a promise that every letter group has only one pronunciation in every context.
blocos.comparacao: English speakers may see ei and say 'ee' or 'ay'. In German, start by trusting ei = eye and ie = ee. Train both directions: see the spelling and predict the sound; hear the sound and choose the spelling.

erros.motivo: Wien has ie /iː/; it means Vienna.

blocos.titulo: Consonant clusters you can read on sight
blocos.explicacao: STEP 1: «sch» sounds /ʃ/ as in English ship: «Schule», «Fisch». STEP 2: «sp» and «st» at the beginning of a native German word or stressed stem normally start with /ʃp/ and /ʃt/: «Sport», «Stein». STEP 3: The two main sounds of «ch» are [ç] after front vowels (as in «ich») and [x] after back vowels (as in «Buch»). English has no exact everyday equivalent to [ç]; Scottish loch is a useful approximation for [x]. STEP 4: «tsch» sounds /tʃ/ as in English church: «Deutsch». STEP 5: «pf», «qu», «ck» and «ng» have their own patterns: «Apfel», «Quelle», «Jacke», «singen». Listen before trying to imitate unfamiliar sounds.
blocos.comparacao: English 'ch' in church is /tʃ/. German «ch» is usually [ç] or [x]; German «tsch» gives you the English church sound. Do not pronounce «ich» as English 'itch'.

erros.motivo: Initial sp in this German word is /ʃp/.

blocos.enunciado: Three-step decoding challenge. (1) Read «Wein» and «Wien» aloud and explain the meaning difference. (2) Read «Schule», «Sport», «Buch» and «ich» without transliteration; identify each consonant pattern. (3) Replay the audio and identify one sound you need to practise again. Say it three times, slowly then naturally.
blocos.exemplo: Wein /vaɪn/ = wine; Wien /viːn/ = Vienna; Schule /ʃ/; Sport /ʃp/; Buch [x]; ich [ç].
